tldr: We propose "CUE", an agentic system where the robot pokes and interacts with the environment itself to uncover friction and restitution that cannot be inferred from images alone, thereby closing the simulator's error. In a billiards task, it improves predictive accuracy by up to 72% over strong baselines without any human intervention.
overview:
The "Real2Sim2Real" paradigm has attracted significant attention: it reconstructs a digital twin (a virtual replica) of an environment inside a simulator using camera images, trains policies there, and transfers them back to the real world. However, contact-rich physical properties, such as coefficients of friction and restitution, cannot be determined from visual appearance alone. This discrepancy in physical behavior between simulation and reality—the "dynamics gap"—has been a major barrier to real-world deployment.

To address this, the authors developed "CUE (Calibration Using Exploration)," an agentic system where a robot actively interacts with its environment to identify simulation parameters. Given only a high-level instruction and operating without human resets of the table, the agent relies on web knowledge and reasoning to build its own vision tracking pipeline and repeatedly probes interactions where its simulation predictions are least accurate.

For validation, the authors set up a billiards environment where contact dynamics heavily dictate outcomes. In simulation experiments (sim-to-sim) across 25 hidden-physics conditions, 30 exploratory shots reduced held-out ball-position error by up to 72% compared to the strongest baseline. Furthermore, they deployed the system on a real mini pool table (sim-to-real), demonstrating the feasibility of fully autonomous physics identification alongside key challenges for the future.
contributions: Proposing "CUE", an agentic system that autonomously performs physical parameter identification and active exploration from only high-level instructions, without relying on human-guided resets or pre-engineered parameter search spaces.
Reducing ball-position prediction error on held-out configurations by up to 72% compared to the strongest existing baselines across 25 unknown physics conditions in a billiards environment.

Uncovering concrete insights and challenges for deploying agentic robotics in real environments—such as the importance of robust vision tools and experimental judgment—through real-world validation on a mini pool table.

sections.heading: Why "touching and probing" is essential for identifying a simulator
sections.summary: Conventional approaches that reconstruct simulators purely from images cannot capture physical properties like contact friction and restitution. This paper proposes an approach where the agent actively intervenes in the environment to refine its physical parameters.
sections.details:
With the recent rise of large-scale, high-fidelity physics simulators and multimodal large language models (MLLMs) possessing strong 3D spatial reasoning, the "Real2Sim2Real" development paradigm has become increasingly practical. The workflow involves scanning a physical environment with cameras, creating a digital twin in simulation, iteratively improving policies via reinforcement learning, and ultimately deploying them onto a real robot. However, this pipeline invariably runs into the "dynamics gap." No matter how visually detailed the scene reconstruction is, if contact dynamics such as friction or restitution coefficients diverge, skills acquired in simulation will not transfer to the physical world.

This study uses billiards as a testbed to examine this challenge. While the geometric shapes of the table and balls can be readily reconstructed from images, modeling contact-driven state transitions like collisions and rolling accurately in advance is extraordinarily difficult.

Conventional dynamics identification methods have predominantly relied on passive learning from offline-collected data. These inherit human behavioral biases and do not allow the agent to actively select which interactions to probe. Even among system identification methods that employ active exploration, most require humans to pre-define the parameter search space and the simulator structure. Such human preconceptions narrow the search range, undermining scalability and generalizability.

CUE (Calibration Using Exploration) was developed to overcome these limitations. CUE actively pokes and probes the environment, predicts interactions, and self-improves its simulation parameters to match collected trajectories. Its goal is to learn unknown physical properties from scratch without any human intervention in the physical environment.

sections.heading: Poking to learn: How CUE works and its experimental findings
sections.summary: Starting from minimal high-level instructions, CUE autonomously builds perception and executes active parameter identification, reducing billiards ball-position error by up to 72% relative to baselines. Real-world deployment also reveals key challenges for agentic systems.
sections.details:
### Method Workflow: From Prior Knowledge to Active Probing
CUE starts with only a high-level instruction: "Reconstruct the scene in simulation and interact with the physical table until you are confident the simulation explains reality. There will be no human resets during exploration, so plan ahead." Guided by this prompt, the agent autonomously designs a data collection plan and a system identification protocol.

First, from initial images, it constructs a MuJoCo model of the table, cushions, pockets, cue stick, and balls. Drawing on its prior knowledge and web searches, it decides which physical parameters are critical, defines their initial ranges, and suggests an initial set of exploratory shots. Next, to compare reality with simulation, it builds its own ball-tracking pipeline from camera feeds. It then reproduces the shots from measured initial states across parallel MuJoCo instances and optimizes parameters using the evolutionary algorithm CMA-ES to minimize trajectory discrepancies. Rather than continuing with random guesswork, the agent iteratively proposes new shots that specifically target interactions where the current simulation's predictions are least accurate.

### Experimental Results: Sim-to-Sim and Real-World Evaluation
Validation was conducted both in sim-to-sim to measure statistical accuracy and in sim-to-real to assess practical feasibility.

In sim-to-sim, MuJoCo billiard environments with hidden physical parameters served as the "real world." The evaluation covered 25 conditions combining 5 table layouts and 5 distinct physical setups. Each method was budgeted up to 30 shots. After 30 shots, the final ball-position error was measured on held-out test configurations. Compared to the strongest baselines (CEM: 3.20 cm, Random Search: 3.20 cm, Uncalibrated: 3.25 cm), CUE achieved 0.91 cm with Opus 5.5 as the backbone (a 72% error reduction) and 1.32 cm with Astra 6.1 (a 59% error reduction).

The authors also deployed CUE to a real mini pool table with unknown physical properties (sim-to-real), verifying that the agent can learn autonomously in the real world.

### Lessons for Truly Solving Real2Sim2Real
The authors identified three key takeaways from the real-world deployment:
- The need for more expressive dynamics models: Microscopic ball scratches or non-uniform surface friction cannot be perceived from camera images, and simple parameter tuning cannot capture them. Combining physics simulation with data-driven models is essential.
- Sound experimental judgment: During extended physical experiments, the agent struggled to balance computational time against interaction budgets. Mechanisms are needed to help the agent decide when to think, act, recalibrate parameters, or backtrack.
- More robust vision tools: Vision pipelines authored by the agent were fragile and sometimes trapped the agent in iterative debugging loops. Robust tools that agents can reliably assemble, verify, and utilize are necessary.

takeaways: Relying solely on visual observations has clear limits for closing the dynamics gap in Real2Sim2Real, making active environmental probing by the agent highly effective.
Even under the constraint of zero human resets, an agent can end-to-end construct its perception pipeline, identify parameters, and plan shots that probe its own weaknesses.

To achieve fully autonomous real-world identification, moving beyond simple physics parameter tuning toward hybrid (physics + data-driven) models, robust vision modules, and meta-level experimental judgment will be key.
limitations: Physical phenomena beyond the simulator's representational capacity—such as micro-scratches on ball surfaces or local irregularities on the table—cannot be captured through parameter identification alone.
Computer vision pipelines generated autonomously by the agent lacked robustness, requiring excessive prompting assistance and trial-and-error to fix.
Safety-driven human fail-safes were still required, leaving open challenges for ensuring safety in completely unmonitored environments.
